question: Does layerwise Hessian sensitivity explain why uniform continual-learning regularization wastes stability budget, and can curvature-inspired layer-adaptive schedules improve EWC-style and pretrained continual learning?

key_findings.claim: Layerwise curvature is strongly heterogeneous, so equal penalties need not protect equal amounts of old-task loss.
key_findings.evidence: Using the top eigenvalue of each diagonal Hessian block as sensitivity, reported condition ratios span 55.1 for ResNet-18, 75.4 for ResNet-34, 195.3 for ResNet-50, 181.4 for ResNet-101, 31.5 for ViT-B, and 22.3 for ViT-L. Profiles also change with pretraining: ViT-B ratios are 31.5 for ImageNet-1K, 14.6 for ImageNet-21K, and 27.4 for MoCoV3, with different hottest layers.

key_findings.claim: Under block-diagonal local quadratic assumptions, the top eigenvalue—not the mean diagonal Fisher—is the correct worst-case scalar sensitivity for a layer.
key_findings.evidence: The paper decomposes quadratic forgetting by Hessian blocks and shows that the mean diagonal can underestimate the top eigenvalue by a factor between 1 and layer dimension. With additional block-diagonal new-task curvature and strong convexity, uniform allocation has a regret lower bound that grows with layer sensitivity ratio, while the worst-case scalar penalty satisfies lambda_l proportional to s_l.

key_findings.claim: A smooth layerwise schedule gives modest gains in one pretrained SLCA setting but does not generalize across pretraining regimes.
key_findings.evidence: On Split-CIFAR100 with ViT-B pretrained on ImageNet-21K, five-seed results improve final accuracy from 91.35+/-0.23 to 91.80+/-0.23 and incremental accuracy from 94.40+/-0.69 to 94.51+/-0.66; the paired t-test p-values are .0018 and .022, while the final-accuracy Wilcoxon p-value is .0625. Under MoCoV3, the schedule scores 84.26+/-0.48 versus default 84.44+/-0.29, with p=.29.

key_findings.claim: Literal use of measured sensitivities fails badly; the practical method succeeds by shrinking and smoothing the theoretically prescribed ratios.
key_findings.evidence: The direct measured-s schedule trails uniform regularization by roughly 4-14 absolute accuracy points in appendix tests. A compressed interpolation improves ResNet-18 to 0.590+/-0.014 from uniform 0.557+/-0.021, but ResNet-50 selects beta=0, i.e. uniform; online remeasurement only restores approximate parity at 0.462+/-0.056 versus 0.453+/-0.034.

key_findings.claim: The block-diagonal approximation is empirically violated and the derived sensitivity bound is often extremely loose.
key_findings.evidence: Adjacent-block coupling ratios reach 1.211 for ResNet-50 and 1.337 for ResNet-101. Direct-displacement comparisons give block-diagonal/full forgetting ratios of 0.71+/-0.16 for ResNet-18 and 0.50+/-0.08 for ResNet-50; although the sensitivity bound holds in 9/9 tests, its ratio to full quadratic forgetting is 780-954, and 2/9 measured actual forgetting values are negative, which a PSD local quadratic cannot represent.

method.core_idea: Estimate each layer's old-task curvature by the dominant eigenvalue of its Hessian block, then allocate stronger continual-learning regularization or smaller effective movement to high-sensitivity layers.
method.mechanism: A local Taylor expansion decomposes forgetting under a block-diagonal Hessian. Power iteration estimates per-layer top eigenvalues, and theory compares a sensitivity-weighted stability budget with uniform penalties. In practice, instead of using raw estimates, the method applies a low-dimensional geometric or interpolated layer schedule, typically protecting early pretrained layers more and allowing later layers to adapt.
assumptions: Old-task forgetting is locally approximated by a positive-semidefinite quadratic around the previous optimum.
Cross-layer Hessian blocks can be ignored or bounded tightly enough for diagonal-block sensitivities to be informative.
Worst-case displacement alignment is the relevant criterion for selecting scalar layer penalties.
Sensitivities measured at one checkpoint and on a small calibration sample remain useful as learning moves away from that point.
A monotone geometric layer order is an adequate proxy even when measured profiles are nonmonotone and pretraining-dependent.

techniques.role: Approximates total old-task loss increase as a sum of layerwise quadratic contributions.
Estimates each layer block's dominant Hessian eigenvalue without materializing the full Hessian.
Derives scalar penalties proportional to layer sensitivity under a minimax displacement model.
Compresses raw curvature ratios into a smooth low-dimensional early-to-late regularization schedule.
Shrinks measured sensitivities toward uniform to avoid starving high-curvature layers of plasticity.
Re-estimates sensitivity after distribution or parameter drift to test whether stale curvature explains failure.

evaluations.setting: MediumCNN on ten-task Split-CIFAR100, three seeds
evaluations.result: Best adaptive setting reached 59.8+/-1.5 versus uniform 57.2+/-1.3; forgetting and backward transfer preferred weaker schedules

evaluations.setting: ViT-B ImageNet-21K pretrained SLCA on Split-CIFAR100, five seeds
ViT-B MoCoV3 pretrained SLCA on Split-CIFAR100, five seeds

evaluations.setting: Direct measured-s penalties in appendix controls
evaluations.result: Literal curvature-proportional schedules underperform uniform by about 4-14 absolute points
Coupling can exceed one; sensitivity bound is 780-954 times full quadratic forgetting despite holding in 9/9 cases

limitations: Author-stated: skip connections, layer normalization, and attention violate the block-diagonal Hessian assumption.

Author-stated: the quadratic account is local, empirical Fisher differs from the Hessian, SLCA correspondence is functional rather than algebraically exact, and no stability guarantee extends beyond a trust region.
Author-stated: curvature is measured at the previous solution but used after parameters move, so stale sensitivity can misallocate regularization.
Reviewer-identified: the flagship practical schedule is a smoothed monotone heuristic, while literal application of the central theorem's measured sensitivities is strongly negative.
Reviewer-identified: evidence is concentrated on image classification, seed counts are small, and the statistically clearest gain is only 0.45 percentage points in one pretraining regime.
Reviewer-identified: the final-accuracy Wilcoxon test does not cross .05 with five seeds, and tuning multiple schedule shapes and strengths increases selection risk.
Reviewer-identified: code was not public at submission, limiting independent reproduction of Hessian measurement and schedule selection.
failure_modes: Raw dominant-eigenvalue ratios can nearly freeze sensitive layers and prevent learning the new task.
Cross-layer curvature can dominate the sum of diagonal blocks, invalidating layer-independent allocation.
Sensitivity profiles can change with pretraining, architecture, task, and time, making one fixed early-to-late schedule wrong.
A monotone geometric schedule cannot represent nonmonotone profiles with sensitive middle or late blocks.
Worst-case eigenvector protection may spend budget on directions the actual new-task gradient never uses.
Noisy power iteration on small calibration batches can exaggerate the dynamic range and reverse layer rankings.
Optimizing average accuracy can worsen forgetting or backward transfer, so the preferred schedule depends on the evaluation objective.
reusable_insights: Audit sensitivity heterogeneity before assuming one regularization coefficient is meaningful across a deep network.
Report raw curvature schedules and compressed practical schedules separately; their performance can have opposite signs.
Measure cross-block coupling and direct realized displacements, not only diagonal-block spectra.
Shrink noisy sensitivity ratios toward uniform and remeasure online when curvature drift is plausible.
Tune layer adaptivity jointly for stability, plasticity, and the metric that matters; final accuracy and forgetting need not agree.
Condition any curvature prescription on gradient alignment, because a large eigenvalue matters only when updates enter that direction.
open_questions: Can an online estimator combine block sensitivity, cross-layer coupling, and actual gradient alignment cheaply enough for continual training?
What trust-region or adaptive-clipping rule turns the local quadratic account into a reliable controller?
Why does compressed monotone scheduling help when literal measured-s allocation fails, and can that gap be predicted?
Do layer-adaptive schedules survive language, multimodal, generative, and reinforcement-learning continual tasks?
How should regularization be allocated when representations can rotate or when normalization creates scale symmetries?
Can preregistered multi-seed studies establish gains beyond one pretraining regime and compare against equally tuned layerwise baselines?

competitive_landscape.title: Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: EWC slows each parameter according to a diagonal Fisher estimate. This paper aggregates curvature at layer blocks and uses dominant Hessian eigenvalues to reason about worst-case movement; its practical schedule is lower-dimensional but loses EWC's per-parameter directionality.

competitive_landscape.title: SLCA: Slow Learner with Classifier Alignment for Continual Learning on a Pre-trained Model
competitive_landscape.difference: SLCA uses a slow pretrained backbone, faster classifier learning, and classifier alignment. Layers Matter interprets and generalizes the slow-learner idea into per-block schedules motivated by curvature, yielding a modest gain for ImageNet-21K pretraining but none for MoCoV3.

competitive_landscape.title: Meta Continual Learning Revisited: Implicitly Enhancing Online Hessian Approximation via Variance Reduction
competitive_landscape.difference: This ICLR 2024 work reframes regularization-based continual learning through online Hessian approximation and improves it with variance reduction. Layers Matter instead focuses on how protection strength should vary across layer blocks using top eigenvalues; it does not provide the same temporal Hessian-estimation mechanism.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: prior regularization methods overlook layerwise sensitivity, and a Hessian-derived allocation principle explains and improves layer-adaptive continual learning. Reviewer inference: EWC already makes protection nonuniform per parameter, SLCA already separates learning rates by model part, and recent work explicitly analyzes Hessian approximation. The distinct contribution is the layer-block top-eigenvalue minimax derivation plus unusually useful diagnostics showing heterogeneity and assumption failure. Practical novelty is weaker: the literal prescription performs poorly, gains rely on compressed heuristic schedules, and the only clear improvement is small and pretraining-specific.
reviewer_notes: The main text and all appendices were read. Results were checked against Tables 1, 5, and 6 and the direct-displacement and negative-schedule appendices. The record deliberately includes cross-block violations, loose bounds, and failed literal schedules. Competitors were verified through primary arXiv or OpenReview pages.
